questions.prompt: In stock index options, how does implied volatility usually change from low strikes to high strikes?
options: It is the same at every strike
It rises from low strikes to high strikes
It is highest at the strike nearest the index
It falls from low strikes to high strikes
questions.explanation: Stock index options show a skew: in the example, implied volatility falls from 27% at strike 80 to 17% at strike 120.

questions.prompt: The put with strike $80 costs $1.91 at its 27% implied volatility, but $0.69 at a flat 20%. What does this gap reflect?
options: An error in the Black-Scholes formula
The market charging for crash risk and fat tails that a flat volatility leaves out
The interest rate being higher for low strikes
questions.explanation: Large falls happen more often than a bell predicts, and buyers pay for protection. So the market prices the $80 put at about 2.77 times its flat-volatility price.

questions.prompt: A normal distribution puts a daily move beyond 5 standard deviations at about once in 6,900 years. In 1987, the S&P 500 fell by about 20 standard deviations in one day. What does this show?
options: Real returns have fat tails: extreme days happen far more often than the normal distribution predicts
The normal distribution fits daily returns well
questions.explanation: A move that size should almost never happen under a bell curve, yet it did. Real returns have more extreme days than the normal distribution allows.
